records.sourceFile: Fatigue and human performance - An updated framework.pdf

paper.citation: Behrens M, Gube M, Chaabene H, Prieske O, Zenon A, Broscheid KC, et al. Fatigue and Human Performance: An Updated Framework. Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: Narrative review that updates the fatigue framework of Enoka and Duchateau. It separates trait fatigue from motor or cognitive task-induced state fatigue, and defines state fatigue as a decrease in motor or cognitive performance and/or an increased perception of fatigue. It adds cognitive performance fatigue and perceived cognitive fatigue to the taxonomy, adds determinants such as effort perception, affective valence and self-regulation, discusses how performance fatigue and perceived fatigue interact, and proposes research recommendations.
paper.tldr: Task-induced fatigue has two interdependent parts, a drop in motor or cognitive performance and a rise in perceived fatigue, and no single factor determines either. When assessing fatigue, measure objective performance and perceived fatigue together, and account for task type, duration and motivation.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors propose a revised taxonomy and framework and discuss the mechanisms of motor and cognitive performance fatigue and perceived fatigue, drawing on studies in healthy, older and clinical populations. The Methods section does not describe a search strategy or study selection process.
paper.findings: In one cited comparison, a 90-minute AX continuous performance test and a 16-minute working-memory dual task both raised perceived cognitive fatigue; the largest visual analogue scale rise was in the individualised dual-task condition, while the AX test produced a larger rise in fatigue and drop in vigor on the Brunel Mood Scale. Perceived cognitive fatigue rose consistently with time on task, whereas cognitive performance declines were often missing when measured on the fatiguing task itself, and a boredom condition produced higher perceived fatigue than an active cognitive task despite lower effort ratings. In motor-cognitive dual-task studies, time to exhaustion in submaximal motor tasks was shorter with a concurrent cognitive task, tended to be shorter under high than low cognitive load, and knee extensor voluntary activation fell more in dual-task than single motor task conditions.
paper.limitations: The review does not state how studies were selected, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. The framework is a conceptual update, and the authors note that the interdependence of performance and perceived fatigue, and the relative weight of each determinant, remain to be quantified. Many cited studies used laboratory tasks or clinical and older-adult samples rather than athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Measure objective performance and perceived fatigue together when assessing fatigue, because the reviewed studies show perceived fatigue rising even when task performance does not decline. Consider the cognitive load, duration and the person's interest in a task when judging perceived cognitive fatigue. The cited dual-task and prior-cognitive-task studies suggest cognitive demands can shorten time to exhaustion in a motor task, though this evidence comes from laboratory tasks rather than sport.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the framework suggests that sessions which combine physical and cognitive demands may produce fatigue that a physical test alone would miss. The review gives no training prescription and does not test any athlete intervention.
paper.rtp: The framework is not designed to guide return to sport, and it does not provide validated criteria for judging fatigue recovery after injury. Its use in return-to-sport decisions would be an extrapolation beyond the review.

records.sourceFile: Fiber-type traps - Revisiting common misconceptions about skeletal muscle fiber types with application to motor control, biomechanics, physiology, and biology.pdf

paper.citation: Blemker SS, Brooks SV, Esser KA, Saul KR. Fiber-type traps: revisiting common misconceptions about skeletal muscle fiber types with application to motor control, biomechanics, physiology, and biology. J Appl Physiol. 2024;136:109-121.
paper.abstract: A review that brings together muscle research fields to examine three common fibre-type assumptions: that classification by myosin isoform and by oxidative capacity are equivalent, that fibre cross-sectional area is a surrogate for myosin isoform or oxidative capacity, and that muscle force-generating capacity can be inferred from myosin isoform. The authors find that none of these assumptions is universally valid and warn against generalising fibre-type findings across muscles, species or sex.
paper.tldr: Fibre type, oxidative capacity, fibre size and force are related only loosely and vary by muscle, species and sex. Treat claims that infer fatigue resistance, fibre size or strength from a fibre-type label, or fibre type from imaging, with caution.
paper.methods: Narrative review and perspective by four muscle researchers from biomedical engineering, physiology and mechanical engineering backgrounds. It traces the history of each assumption and discusses histochemical, antibody, imaging and mechanical evidence across species. No search strategy or study selection process is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that myosin heavy chain antibody staining is the best available fibre-typing method but gives no information on metabolic properties, and that type IIX fibres have very low oxidative enzyme activity in humans but moderate or high activity in rats and mice. They report wide overlap in cross-sectional area between fibre types, including in human vastus lateralis, and sex differences such as larger type IIA fibres in males but larger type I fibres in females in one biopsy study. A cited meta-analysis of 61 human fibre studies found type IIa fibres produce about 24% higher specific force than type I, but variation between research groups exceeded variation between fibre types, and whole-muscle force depends on architecture, coordination and motor unit recruitment.
paper.limitations: This is a perspective review without a described search method, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Much of the evidence is from animal muscle, and the paper does not test any of its points in athletes or training studies.
paper.practicalImplications: When interpreting biopsy, imaging or marketing claims about fibre type, check how fibre type was measured and in which muscle, species and sex, because the authors show these change the result. Do not treat fibre cross-sectional area or imaging measures such as diffusion tensor imaging as a stand-in for fibre type.
paper.athleteDev: The review cautions against predicting an athlete's strength, fatigue resistance or fibre size from a fibre-type label, noting that whole-muscle force depends on architecture, coordination and recruitment as well as fibre type. It gives no training prescription.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury or return to sport and cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Flywheel resistance training promotes unique muscle architectural and performance‐related adaptations in young adults.pdf

paper.citation: Banks NF, Berry AC, Rogers EM, Jenkins NDM. Flywheel resistance training promotes unique muscle architectural and performance-related adaptations in young adults. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-14.
paper.abstract: Randomized, non-exercise-controlled 10-week study in 31 physically active young adults comparing volume-matched total-body traditional resistance training (TRT), flywheel resistance training (FWRT) and a habitual-activity control (CON). TRT and FWRT both increased maximal isometric torque and fat-free mass compared with CON. FWRT increased fascicle length, countermovement jump and broad jump relative to CON, while TRT increased pennation angle and produced larger free-weight 1RM gains than FWRT.
paper.tldr: In physically active young adults, 10 weeks of volume-matched flywheel or traditional resistance training gave similar gains in isometric strength and fat-free mass compared with control. Flywheel training also improved fascicle length and jump performance relative to control, while traditional training produced larger free-weight 1RM squat and bench gains.
paper.methods: Thirty-one physically active adults were randomized to TRT, FWRT or CON. Both training groups completed three sessions per week for 10 weeks of a periodized total-body program (squat, bench press, deadlift, row plus assistance work), with load on FWRT prescribed from work in joules. Outcomes were isometric leg extension torque, 1RM free-weight squat and bench, 3-repetition flywheel work, ultrasound muscle size, fascicle length and pennation angle, body composition, and countermovement and broad jump; group by visit mixed linear models were used with Tukey post hoc tests.
paper.findings: Compared with CON, TRT and FWRT both increased maximal isometric torque (TRT +78.6 Nm, p=0.014; FWRT +56.1 Nm, p=0.023) and fat-free mass (TRT +1.72 kg, p=0.008; FWRT +1.44 kg, p=0.032), with no difference between the two training groups. TRT increased free-weight squat 1RM more than FWRT (+43.3 kg, p<0.001) and CON (+79.3 kg), and bench 1RM more than FWRT (+15.6 kg, p<0.001) and CON (+21.8 kg); FWRT improved squat 1RM versus CON (+36.0 kg, p=0.002) but not bench 1RM (p=0.25), and improved flywheel squat and bench 3Wmax versus CON but not versus TRT. FWRT increased fascicle length (+1.33 cm vs CON, p=0.002), countermovement jump (+2.37 cm vs CON, p=0.048) and broad jump (+47.5 cm vs CON, p=0.007), while TRT increased pennation angle more than both CON (+3.01 deg) and FWRT (+1.81 deg); change in fascicle length correlated with change in broad jump (r=0.49, p=0.005) and, not significantly, countermovement jump (r=0.35, p=0.054). Proximal vastus lateralis size increased with TRT only versus CON (+3.71 cm2, p=0.02), and distal vastus lateralis size increased with FWRT only versus CON (+3.29 cm2, p=0.005).
paper.limitations: Groups were small (8 to 12) and the authors state the study was not powered for all comparisons or for sex-specific effects. The direct FWRT versus TRT differences were not significant for distal vastus lateralis size (p=0.41), proximal vastus lateralis size (p=0.056), countermovement jump (p=0.19) or broad jump (p=0.22). Only isometric and flywheel-specific strength were tested; velocity was recorded for FWRT but not TRT, and FWRT received real-time work feedback that may have encouraged faster reps. Participants were physically active rather than trained athletes. The reported 95% CI for the FWRT versus CON isometric torque difference (-27.92 to 140.08 Nm) crosses zero despite p=0.023.
paper.practicalImplications: For physically active young adults on a volume-matched total-body block, flywheel and free-weight training gave similar isometric strength and lean mass gains, so equipment access and preference can guide the choice. If free-weight squat or bench 1RM is the target, traditional training produced larger gains. Flywheel training improved jumps versus control, but its jump advantage over free weights was not statistically significant and should be tested in athletes before it is relied on.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: flywheel training matched free-weight training for isometric strength and lean mass gains in physically active young adults, and improved jump performance versus control. Free-weight training gave larger squat and bench 1RM gains. The jump difference between the two training modes was not significant, and the sample was not athletes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study tested healthy, physically active adults and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Forces experienced at different levels of the musculoskeletal system during horizontal decelerations.pdf

paper.citation: Verheul J, Harper D, Robinson MA. Forces experienced at different levels of the musculoskeletal system during horizontal decelerations. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024. Published online 15 Nov 2024.
paper.abstract: Team-sport athletes performed maximal-effort horizontal decelerations while full-body kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded. A musculoskeletal model estimated whole-body, joint-level and tissue-level loads across the lower limb. The authors report large external forces, large hip, ankle and knee joint moments and contact forces, and high eccentric force requirements in several muscles, which they suggest helps explain why decelerations are among the most demanding movements in team sports.
paper.tldr: Maximal horizontal decelerations load the hip, ankle and knee heavily, with peak hip and ankle contact forces of about 14 and 24 body weights and high eccentric demand on the tibialis anterior, soleus, quadriceps and gluteal muscles. The authors suggest these patterns may guide deceleration-focused training, but the sample is small and the muscle forces are modelled.
paper.methods: Fifteen recreational team-sport athletes landed one foot on a force platform during the first or second braking step after a maximal sprint, completing at least ten valid trials, with 161 trials analysed. Ten cameras and 76 markers recorded kinematics, and an OpenSim full-body model with 80 muscle-tendon units was scaled to each athlete to estimate joint moments, contact forces and muscle forces by static optimization.
paper.findings: Peak vertical and anteroposterior ground reaction forces were 4.48 plus or minus 1.11 and -1.67 plus or minus 0.27 body weights. Peak hip extension moment was -9.93 plus or minus 4.07 Nm/kg in the first quarter of contact, and mean peak ankle, knee and hip contact forces were 24.49, 12.86 and 13.76 body weights. Nine of twelve muscles acted eccentrically, with the quadriceps lengthening through the whole contact phase and the hamstrings not lengthening; peak tibialis anterior force was 2.95 plus or minus 1.07 body weights. Peak patellar and Achilles tendon forces were 7.42 and 5.58 body weights, which the authors judge no greater than those in common running. The Discussion reports vertical forces about 1.5 to 3 times, and horizontal forces up to about four times, those in accelerated or constant-speed running.
paper.limitations: Only 15 recreational players were tested, and the authors note that sex and athletic experience may change the loading patterns. Muscle and contact forces are estimated with a Hill-type model and static optimization, which does not capture history-dependent muscle behaviour, so tissue loads are model estimates. The abstract states horizontal forces were up to six times those in running, while the Discussion gives up to four times; this summary uses the Discussion figure. Only the first or second braking step after a sprint was analysed.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that eccentric capacity of the tibialis anterior, soleus and quadriceps, and maximal force capacity of the gluteus maximus, may be relevant for athletes who perform many horizontal decelerations. Their data do not identify which training changes improve deceleration performance, so these are hypotheses to test rather than prescriptions. The tendon forces were not higher than in common running, so decelerations alone do not clearly raise patellar or Achilles tendon load beyond running.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the authors describe horizontal deceleration as a key team-sport performance demand and suggest that the loading data can inform deceleration-specific training. They also state that which force characteristics to target, and whether targeted interventions improve deceleration, remain unresolved.
paper.rtp: Limited application: the athletes were healthy and injury-free for at least six months, so the study does not describe return-to-sport loading. The authors suggest the high loads could contribute to injury risk, including ACL and shank injuries, but this is an inference from modelled loads, not a tested injury outcome, and it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: From Tissue to System - What Constitutes an Appropriate Response to Loading.pdf

paper.citation: Gabbett TJ, Oetter E. From Tissue to System: What Constitutes an Appropriate Response to Loading? Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes the typical response of muscle, tendon, bone and cartilage to training load and the time each needs to recover before a similar load. The authors propose a conceptual framework with typical recovery timeframes, from about 30 minutes for cartilage to 48 to 72 hours or more for some high-stress loads. They conclude that load and response data should be interpreted together within an athlete monitoring framework.
paper.tldr: Recovery time varies by tissue, from about 30 minutes for cartilage to 48 to 72 hours or more after high-stress muscle loading, so one rest rule does not fit every tissue. The authors suggest reading training load alongside athlete responses and readiness measures.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed searches using combinations of training, load, tissue, response and recovery terms, with hand-checking of related systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Only English-language, peer-reviewed studies in humans were included. The text describes no formal screening or quality-appraisal process.
paper.findings: The review presents time courses rather than new data. Examples include bone mechanosensitivity falling after about 20 loading cycles and recovering over about 8 hours in a cited animal study, and reactive tendons benefiting from a 48-hour refractory period. A cited study reported that sprint-related performance decrements lasted 48 to 72 hours, and a cited meta-analysis reported tendon stiffness gains with contraction intensities of at least 70% of maximal voluntary contraction or 1RM (effect size 0.90 versus 0.04).
paper.limitations: As a narrative review with no formal selection, appraisal or pooled analysis, the timelines are the authors' synthesis. The 20-cycle bone figure cites an animal study (reference 5), and the authors state that exact recovery durations are not established for some tissues, such as rapid eccentric muscle contractions. The example microcycles are described as illustrations, not tested programs.
paper.practicalImplications: Separate high-stress sessions, such as maximal sprinting or heavy eccentric work, by at least 48 to 72 hours, as the review's example microcycles do. Schedule lower-body strength or plyometric work 4 to 8 hours after running when bone-centric loading is wanted. Interpret load alongside soreness, fatigue and readiness measures rather than judging a session from one number.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review's tissue timelines to sequence high-stress and low-stress sessions, and check readiness data before repeating a high-stress dose. The polarized weekly plans are offered as examples of how to combine low-stress aerobic work with a small number of high-intensity sessions.
paper.rtp: The review gives rehabilitation guidance, such as training around an injured tissue and maintaining systemic loading during unloading. It advises that athletes with bone stress injuries be pain-free during daily activity for 5 consecutive days before a return-to-run program, citing one source. It does not test return-to-sport outcomes, so its tissue timelines should not be used as return-to-play clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Genetic variants in myostatin and its receptors promote elite athlete status.pdf

paper.citation: Leońska-Duniec A, Borczyk M, Korostyński M, Massidda M, Maculewicz E, Cięszczyk P. Genetic variants in myostatin and its receptors promote elite athlete status. BMC Genomics. 2023;24:761.
paper.abstract: Myostatin (MSTN) and its receptors ACVR2A and ACVR2B were sequenced by whole-genome sequencing in 102 elite Polish athletes and 41 controls. Two variants that were relatively common in athletes, MSTN rs11333758 and ACVR2A rs3764955, were then genotyped in 330 athletes and 365 controls. Genotypes were associated with competition level and discipline, most strongly in mixed-sport high-elite athletes, where a gene-gene interaction was also found.
paper.tldr: A small Polish genetic association study reports that some MSTN and ACVR2A genotypes differ between elite athletes and controls, mainly in subgroup analyses. The results are hypothesis-generating and do not support genetic testing for athlete selection.
paper.methods: Whole-genome sequencing of MSTN, ACVR2A and ACVR2B was done in 102 elite athletes (101 male, 1 female; sprint/power n = 53, endurance n = 49) and 41 controls (23 female, 18 male). Two SNPs were then genotyped by TaqMan assay in 330 athletes (endurance 101, mixed-sport 138, sprint/power 91) and 365 non-training students, tested under codominant, dominant, recessive and overdominant models with Bonferroni correction and epistasis tested with the W-test.
paper.findings: No variant differed significantly between all athletes and controls, or between discipline groups, after correction in the sequencing analysis. In genotyping, ACVR2A rs3764955 heterozygotes were less common among elite athletes than controls (overdominant model, corrected p = 0.043), and MSTN rs11333758 deletion homozygotes (-/-) were more common among high-elite athletes (recessive model, OR 4.39, p = 0.004). In mixed-sport high-elite athletes, the MSTN -/- genotype was more common (recessive model, OR 8.53, corrected p = 0.0027), no athlete carried the ACVR2A GC plus MSTN AA combination (controls 28%; Fisher p = 0.005), and the interaction test was significant (p = 0.0057).
paper.limitations: Whole-cohort and discipline-level comparisons were not significant, so the positive results rest on subgroup analyses with small cells; the mixed-sport high-elite group has 17 athletes (Table 6) and some genotype-combination cells hold 0 to 6 athletes. Bonferroni correction was applied for the two genotyped variants only, not for the four genetic models and multiple subgroups, and subgroups were far below the 329 per group from the authors' own sample size calculation. Athletes and controls differ in age (27.8 vs 22 years) and sex composition (25% vs 42% female), sex-specific effects were not tested, and the abstract's statement that CC and GG carriers were more likely to be high-elite rests on a non-significant result (overdominant p = 0.067).
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use these genotypes to select, rank or predict athletes, because the study reports no predictive accuracy and the associations are subgroup-level in one Polish cohort. The paper is best used as a research lead on myostatin pathway variation in elite athletes.
paper.athleteDev: These MSTN and ACVR2A variants should not be used to select or predict athletes. The associations are small subgroup findings that have not been replicated.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It examined genotype and competition level in healthy elite athletes and controls, not injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Gluteal Muscle Forces during Hip-Focused Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation Exercises.pdf

paper.citation: Collings TJ, Bourne MN, Barrett RS, Meinders E, Gonçalves BAM, Shield AJ, et al. Gluteal Muscle Forces during Hip-Focused Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation Exercises. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023;55(4):650-660.
paper.abstract: Eight hip-focused exercises were performed with body weight and with a 12RM load by 14 female footballers, and gluteal muscle forces were estimated with an EMG-informed neuromusculoskeletal model. Exercises were ranked and grouped into four tiers for each gluteal muscle. Loading at 12RM increased peak muscle force for all exercises, and the size of the increase varied by exercise and muscle.
paper.tldr: In 14 female footballers, modelled gluteal forces were ranked across eight hip exercises, and adding a 12RM load raised peak force for each one. The forces are model estimates from a single session, and the study reports no training or injury outcomes.
paper.methods: Eight hip-focused exercises were performed with body weight only and with a 12RM load by 14 female footballers aged 18 to 32. Motion capture, ground reaction forces and surface EMG from 12 muscles were used as inputs to an EMG-informed OpenSim model that estimated gluteus maximus, medius and minimus forces, with exercises grouped into tiers by k-means clustering and loaded versus body weight differences reported with 95% CIs.
paper.findings: Tier 1 exercises for gluteus maximus were loaded split squat (95% CI 495 to 688 N), loaded single-leg RDL (500 to 655 N) and loaded single-leg hip thrust (505 to 640 N). For gluteus medius, the top tier was body weight side plank (338 to 483 N), loaded single-leg squat (278 to 422 N) and loaded single-leg RDL (283 to 405 N), and for gluteus minimus it was loaded single-leg RDL (267 to 389 N) and body weight side plank (272 to 382 N). Adding the 12RM load increased mean peak force for every exercise, by 48 to 150 N for gluteus maximus, 62 to 121 N for gluteus medius and 28 to 88 N for gluteus minimus, and peak force coincided with maximum fiber length in five of seven dynamic exercises.
paper.limitations: The main limitation is the generic musculoskeletal model, whose moment arms come from a male model and were not personalized for female participants. The muscle forces were not validated against in vivo measures; the model was only checked against inverse-dynamics joint moments and surface EMG (median errors under 3.5 N·m and 16%). The sample is 14 female footballers from mixed codes, movement speed was fixed at about 30 degrees per second, and the outputs are model estimates from one session, not training or injury outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: The modelled tier rankings can help match exercises to the gluteal muscle being targeted, and adding external load raised modelled force for every exercise, although some loaded exercises still produced less force than other body weight exercises. The study does not show that these forces produce strength, hypertrophy or injury-reduction gains, so the rankings guide mechanical loading rather than prescribe a programme.
paper.athleteDev: Use the tier rankings to choose exercises for the gluteal muscle being trained, and load them externally where possible. The study does not show that the forces produce strength or hypertrophy gains, and it was done in 14 female footballers.
paper.rtp: The participants had no current lower-limb injury, and no post-injury data were collected, so the study cannot establish which exercises are safe or effective in rehabilitation. The authors suggest the rankings may inform rehabilitation goals, which would need to be tested in injured patients.

records.sourceFile: Greater effects by performing a small number of eccentric contractions daily than a larger number of them once a week.pdf

paper.citation: Yoshida R, Sato S, Kasahara K, Murakami Y, Murakoshi F, Aizawa K, et al. Greater effects by performing a small number of eccentric contractions daily than a larger number of them once a week. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2022.
paper.abstract: Thirty-six healthy adults were placed in three groups of 12 for four weeks of maximal eccentric elbow flexor training: one set of six contractions once a week, one set of six on five days a week, or five sets of six once a week. Strength rose significantly only in the five-day group, and muscle thickness rose in both the five-day and once-weekly 30-contraction groups.
paper.tldr: In 36 young adults, only the group doing six maximal eccentric elbow flexor contractions on five days a week gained significant strength, while the group doing the same weekly total in one session did not, and muscle thickness rose in both of those groups. The study is small, non-randomized and limited to the elbow flexors over four weeks.
paper.methods: Thirty-six healthy university students with no regular arm resistance training in the previous six months were placed into three groups of 12 for four weeks: six contractions once a week, six contractions on five days a week, or five sets of six once a week. Maximal isometric, concentric and eccentric elbow flexor torque on an isokinetic dynamometer, and biceps brachii plus brachialis thickness by ultrasound, were measured before and after training and compared among groups with split-plot ANOVA.
paper.findings: Group-by-time interactions were significant for all averaged torque measures, and post hoc tests showed significant increases only in the six-contractions, five-day group: MVC-ISO 9.3 ± 5.5%, MVC-CON 11.1 ± 7.4% and MVC-ECC 13.5 ± 11.5% (d = 0.33 to 0.49). The once-weekly six-contraction and once-weekly 30-contraction groups showed no significant strength change, although the 30-contraction group did the same weekly number of contractions as the five-day group. Muscle thickness increased in the five-day group (10.3 ± 4.4% in Results) and the once-weekly 30-contraction group (8.0 ± 5.8%), with no significant difference between these two groups (p = 0.40).
paper.limitations: Participants were placed into groups with no description of randomization, groups were 12 people each, 24 of the 36 participants were men, and post-training tests were taken 3 to 9 days after the last session because of COVID-19 restrictions. The Results give the five-day thickness change as 10.3 ± 4.4% while the Abstract and Discussion give 10.4%, and thickness change cannot separate hypertrophy from swelling without biopsy or echo-intensity data. The study covered once versus five times a week over four weeks, the elbow flexors only, used an isokinetic dynamometer, and had no neural measures.
paper.practicalImplications: For untrained adults, spreading six maximal eccentric contractions across five days gave strength gains that once-weekly training did not, even with the same weekly total, so the spread of the work over the week may matter. The study does not test athletes or other muscle groups, and maximal eccentric work needs an isokinetic dynamometer or similar device.
paper.athleteDev: Spreading a small number of maximal eccentric contractions across the week raised strength in untrained adults more than the same weekly total done once. The study does not test athletes, sport movements or lower-limb training, so it cannot be applied to athletic performance directly.
paper.rtp: The participants were healthy young adults, and no injured or rehabilitating people were studied. The authors note that maximal eccentric contractions may be unsafe for older or clinical populations, so the study does not establish a rehabilitation or return-to-sport protocol.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring Eccentric Strengthening   Program- Does Training Volume Matter-.pdf

paper.citation: Lacome M, Avrillon S, Cholley Y, Simpson BM, Guilhem G, Buchheit M. Hamstring Eccentric Strengthening Program: Does Training Volume Matter? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2019 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Nineteen elite U19 soccer players were randomised to low-volume (one set, 10 repetitions per week) or high-volume (four sets, 40 repetitions per week) eccentric hamstring training, then crossed over during a 15-week in-season period. Knee-flexor eccentric strength and biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus fascicle length were measured with a NordBord and ultrasound at pre, mid and post-training. The authors conclude that low-volume training is as effective as high-volume training for strength and fascicle length in this group.
paper.tldr: In elite youth soccer players, 10 eccentric hamstring repetitions per week gave strength and fascicle-length gains similar to 40 repetitions per week over 6 weeks. The trial was small, had no control group and did not measure injury.
paper.methods: Nineteen U19 academy players were block-randomised into two groups that completed 6 weeks of either low-volume (1 set of 4 Nordic repetitions and 6 stiff-leg deadlifts) or high-volume (4 sets) training, then crossed over after a 1-week break. Eccentric knee-flexor strength was measured with a NordBord, and biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus fascicle lengths with panoramic ultrasound, at pre, mid (week 7) and post (week 15) testing.
paper.findings: Knee-flexor eccentric strength rose about 11% from pre to mid-training in both groups (low volume +11.3%, high volume +11.4%), with biceps femoris long head fascicles about 4.5 to 4.8% longer and semimembranosus fascicles about 4.3 to 6.3% longer. There was no clear between-group difference in the changes. In the second block, strength and biceps femoris long head length did not change substantially, and the Results report a possibly slightly greater semimembranosus change in the high-volume group.
paper.limitations: The sample was small (9 versus 10 players) with no no-training control group, so the study compares two eccentric doses rather than training against none, and both exercises were given together, so their separate effects cannot be determined. Fascicle length was measured with a panoramic ultrasound algorithm the authors say needs validation, and inference used magnitude-based probabilities rather than significance testing. The group baseline values in Table 1 and the phase 1 PRE values in Table 2 appear swapped between groups, and the abstract does not mention the possible phase 2 semimembranosus difference reported in the Results.
paper.practicalImplications: In-season, a 10-repetition weekly eccentric dose can be considered when fixture congestion limits time for high-volume work, because it produced gains similar to the 40-repetition dose in this group. It should not be presented as a proven injury-prevention dose, since injuries were not measured.
paper.athleteDev: Elite youth soccer players in season gained knee-flexor strength and fascicle length from a low weekly eccentric dose, with no clear between-group difference from four times the volume in this small sample. When the high-volume group dropped to 10 repetitions per week, strength and fascicle length did not change substantially over the next 6 weeks, which the authors read as maintenance.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested healthy players only, so it should not be used to set strength or fascicle-length criteria for clearance.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring Muscle-Tendon Geometric Adaptations to Resistance Training Using the Hip Extension and Nordic Hamstring Exercises.pdf

paper.citation: Lazarczuk SL, Collings TJ, Hams AH, Timmins RG, Shield AJ, Barrett RS, et al. Hamstring Muscle-Tendon Geometric Adaptations to Resistance Training Using the Hip Extension and Nordic Hamstring Exercises. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14728.
paper.abstract: Thirty recreationally active men were randomised to 10 weeks of Nordic exercise, hip extension or control training (10 per group), with MRI of both thighs before and after. Hip extension increased the biceps femoris long head muscle volume-to-interface area ratio, tendon and aponeurosis size changed little, and hamstring muscle size increased in specific regions.
paper.tldr: Ten weeks of Nordic or hip extension training increased hamstring muscle size in specific regions but did little to tendon or aponeurosis size. Hip extension raised the biceps femoris long head muscle-to-aponeurosis ratio, which the authors suggest could affect strain at the musculotendinous junction.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a three-arm randomised controlled trial. Thirty recreationally active men were allocated to control, Nordic or hip extension groups (10 each) and trained twice weekly for 10 weeks, with progressive loading. Thigh MRI was acquired about 1 week before and after training, with manual segmentation of muscle, free tendon and aponeurosis, linear mixed models, and statistical parametric mapping for regional cross-sectional area.
paper.findings: Hip extension produced a larger increase in the BFlh muscle volume-to-interface area ratio than the Nordic (mean difference 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.19, p = 0.03) and control (0.12, 0.03 to 0.22, p = 0.009) groups, while change in BFlh interface area did not differ between groups. Compared with control, semitendinosus cross-sectional area increased in mid-muscle regions with both exercises, and BFlh increased in mid-muscle regions with hip extension. The only significant free tendon difference was a larger semimembranosus increase in the Nordic than the hip extension group (0.06 cm3, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.11), which the authors say was within the standard error of measurement.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, the training dose was a single 10-week programme, and tendon material properties were not measured. MRI slices 10 mm thick could not resolve the proximal semitendinosus tendon. The abstract and Results disagree on the comparator for the semimembranosus free tendon result (control vs hip extension) and on one confidence limit (0.007 vs 0.01), and the Discussion describes BFlh mid-muscle hypertrophy after Nordic training that the regional Results do not show.
paper.practicalImplications: Hip extension increased biceps femoris long head muscle size relative to its aponeurosis interface, whereas the Nordic exercise did not. Because 10 weeks of either exercise produced only limited tendon or aponeurosis change, programmes aiming at tendon adaptation may need longer or higher-strain loading.
paper.athleteDev: Exercise choice changes the ratio between hamstring muscle size and its aponeurosis, and hip extension raised that ratio in this sample. Staff should not assume either exercise builds hamstring tendon or aponeurosis within a 10-week block.
paper.rtp: The sample was uninjured recreationally active men, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Any injury-risk link through the musculotendinous junction remains a hypothesis.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring strength and architectural adaptations following inertial flywheel resistance training.pdf

paper.citation: Presland JD, Opar DA, Williams MD, Hickey JT, Maniar N, Dow CL, et al. Hamstring strength and architectural adaptations following inertial flywheel resistance training. J Sci Med Sport. 2020.
paper.abstract: Twenty recreationally active males completed 6 weeks of flywheel leg-curl training, either conventional (n=10) or with an eccentric bias (n=10), followed by 4 weeks of detraining. The eccentric-bias group showed a 14 +/- 5% increase in biceps femoris long head fascicle length after training, which fell by 13 +/- 4% after detraining. The conventional group showed no change in fascicle length, and neither group showed changes in eccentric or isometric knee flexor strength or rate of force development.
paper.tldr: Eccentrically biased flywheel leg curls lengthened biceps femoris fascicles in 6 weeks, but the gain was lost after 4 weeks without training. Strength did not change in either group.
paper.methods: Randomised, stratified trial with two training groups. The conventional group trained one leg concentrically and eccentrically; the eccentric-bias group trained both legs concentrically but only one leg eccentrically, with the other leg as a within-person control. Fascicle length, pennation angle and muscle thickness were measured by 2D ultrasound weekly, and eccentric Nordic strength, isometric strength and rate of force development were tested before, after training and after detraining.
paper.findings: In the eccentric-bias group, the trained leg's fascicle length rose 14 +/- 5% (p<0.001, d=1.98) and was 1.4 cm longer than the concentric-only leg (95% CI 0.8 to 2.1 cm). This gain reversed by 13 +/- 4% after detraining. The conventional group showed no fascicle change (-0.5 +/- 0.8%). Eccentric strength, isometric strength and rate of force development showed no significant group-by-leg interaction, and pennation angle fell by 1.9 degrees in the eccentric-trained leg relative to the concentric-only leg.
paper.limitations: The sample was 20 recreationally active men with no lower-limb injury in the previous 36 months, and no injury outcome was measured. Eccentric strength was tested bilaterally while training was unilateral, fascicle length was estimated from a 2D extrapolation equation, only the biceps femoris long head was measured, and the two groups used different flywheel inertias (0.05 vs 0.1 kg.m2). Two authors have a patent and commercial or research ties to the NordBord device used for testing.
paper.practicalImplications: Where flywheel leg curls are used, adding an eccentric bias to one leg lengthened biceps femoris fascicles in this sample, while the conventional prescription did not. The gain was lost within 4 weeks without the eccentric stimulus, so the stimulus has to be maintained. The study did not show any strength change or injury effect, and it did not test athletes.
paper.athleteDev: In recreationally active men, eccentrically biased flywheel leg curls changed fascicle length without changing strength or rate of force development. Whether athletes respond the same way is untested.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport: it measured no injured athletes, no rehabilitation outcomes and no time to return. It also does not show that fascicle lengthening reduces re-injury risk, only that the two are plausibly linked.

records.sourceFile: Hamstrings Muscle Architecture and Morphology Following 6 Weeks of an Eccentrically-Biased Romanian Deadlift or Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention.pdf

paper.citation: Crawford SK, Sandberg C, Vlisides J, Thompson Q, Mosiman SJ, Heiderscheit BC, et al. Hamstrings muscle architecture and morphology following 6 weeks of an eccentrically-biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise intervention. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Thirty-two physically active young adults were randomly assigned to a 6-week eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise programme, followed by 2 weeks of detraining. Biceps femoris long head fascicle length increased by 0.80 cm (9%) and pennation angle decreased by 1.2 degrees (10%) after training, and both returned to near baseline after detraining. Anatomical cross-sectional area of the hamstrings increased by 10% after training and remained elevated after detraining, with no differences between the two exercises on any measure.
paper.tldr: Over six weeks, an eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift and a Nordic hamstring exercise produced similar changes in biceps femoris fascicle length, pennation angle and hamstring cross-sectional area. Fascicle length and pennation angle returned to baseline within two weeks of stopping, while cross-sectional area stayed slightly elevated.
paper.methods: Single-blinded randomised trial. Participants were randomised to Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise, trained twice weekly for 6 weeks with matched volume, eccentric tempo and RPE-based loading, and had a 2-week detraining period. Extended-field-of-view ultrasound measured biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and muscle thickness at proximal, mid-belly and distal sites, and anatomical cross-sectional area of three hamstring muscles. Linear mixed models with intention-to-treat analysis were used.
paper.findings: Across both groups, fascicle length increased by 0.80 cm (95% CI 0.6 to 1.0) after training and fell by 0.72 cm after detraining, with no difference from baseline at detraining. Pennation angle fell by 1.2 degrees after training. Hamstring cross-sectional area increased by 0.78 cm2 after training and was still 0.35 cm2 above baseline after detraining. No between-group differences were found for fascicle length (p=0.55), pennation angle (p=0.74), muscle thickness (p=0.48) or cross-sectional area (p=0.60). A location-by-group interaction for fascicle length (p=0.01) did not show differences at any individual site.
paper.limitations: The sample was 32 physically active young adults, not defined as athletes, there was no non-training control group, and the study lasted only 6 weeks. The Romanian deadlift included a concentric return phase and so is less eccentric than the Nordic exercise. Some reported confidence intervals do not match their estimates (cross-sectional area decrease after detraining given as -0.43 cm2 [0.10, 0.76]; muscle thickness group difference -0.06 [-0.12, 0.25] cm), so these values should be checked against the final published version.
paper.practicalImplications: Both exercises produced similar fascicle length, pennation angle and cross-sectional area changes in this sample, so either can be used for these adaptations; the study did not compare tolerance or soreness. Fascicle length and pennation angle changes were lost within two weeks of stopping, so the stimulus needs to continue to keep them. The study did not measure injury or strength.
paper.athleteDev: Over six weeks, an eccentrically biased Romanian deadlift or Nordic hamstring exercise produced similar fascicle length, pennation angle and cross-sectional area changes in physically active adults. Muscle thickness did not change with either exercise, and no strength outcome was measured.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and no return-to-sport or re-injury outcomes, and it measured only muscle architecture in healthy, physically active adults.

records.sourceFile: Hamstrings hypertrophy is specific to the training exercise - Nordic hamstring vs lengthend state eccentric training.pdf

paper.citation: Maeo S, Balshaw TG, Nin DZ, Mc Dermott EJ, Osborne T, Cooper NB, et al. Hamstrings hypertrophy is specific to the training exercise: Nordic hamstring versus lengthened state eccentric training. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Forty-two healthy young men completed 12 weeks of Nordic hamstring training or lengthened state eccentric training on a weight-stack machine, or served as controls. Lengthened state eccentric training produced larger increases in whole-hamstring and biceps femoris long head muscle volume and in biceps femoris aponeurosis area than Nordic hamstring training, while Nordic hamstring training produced larger increases in the knee flexors that do not extend the hip. Maximum eccentric torque rose by 17% after lengthened state eccentric training, compared with 4% in controls. The authors conclude that lengthened state eccentric training is superior for hamstring hypertrophy.
paper.tldr: Twelve weeks of lengthened state eccentric training on a weight-stack machine grew the biceps femoris more than Nordic hamstring training, while Nordic training grew the knee flexors that do not cross the hip more. Neither sprint performance nor injury was measured.
paper.methods: Participants were allocated to control (1:2 by schedule) or to training groups randomised to lengthened state eccentric training or Nordic hamstring training, for 34 sessions over 12 weeks with progressive load. Axial MRI measured volumes of seven knee flexors and the biceps femoris aponeurosis before and after training, and isometric, concentric and eccentric knee flexion torque were measured in duplicate sessions.
paper.findings: Whole hamstring volume rose 18% after LSET and 11% after NHT, with no change in controls, and the change differed between all three groups (LSET>NHT>CON). BFlh volume rose 19% after LSET and 5% after NHT, and the NHT change in BFlh and semimembranosus did not differ from controls; BFlh aponeurosis area rose 9% after LSET, 3% after NHT and 2% in controls, with only LSET greater than the other groups. Maximum eccentric torque rose 17% after LSET (p=0.002), 11% after NHT (p=0.048) and 4% in controls (p=0.397); only LSET versus controls differed (p=0.009), and LSET versus NHT did not (p=0.237).
paper.limitations: The two regimes differed in equipment, hip position, unilateral versus bilateral eccentric work and the presence of concentric work, so the study did not isolate one variable. Controls were allocated by schedule, not at random, and isometric and concentric torque also rose in controls, suggesting learning effects. Sprint performance and injury were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In untrained young men, a machine-based lengthened-state programme grew the biceps femoris more than Nordic training over 12 weeks, while Nordic training grew the knee flexors that do not cross the hip more. Choose the exercise to match the muscle goal, and do not assume either one prevents injury or improves sprinting.
paper.athleteDev: The study shows different hypertrophy patterns between two knee flexor programmes in untrained men. The authors suggest a sprint benefit, but the study did not measure sprinting.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and measured no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Heat Acclimation by Post-Exercise Hot Water Immersion in the Morning Reduces Thermal Strain During Morning and Afternoon Exercise-Heat-Stress.pdf

paper.citation: Zurawlew MJ, Mee JA, Walsh NP. Heat acclimation by post-exercise hot water immersion in the morning reduces thermal strain during morning and afternoon exercise-heat-stress. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Ten recreationally active men completed exercise-heat stress tests in the morning and afternoon before and after six days of morning post-exercise hot water immersion. Rest and exercise rectal temperature, heart rate, perceived exertion and thermal sensation fell after heat acclimation, and the reductions did not differ between morning and afternoon tests.
paper.tldr: Six days of hot water immersion after morning exercise lowered core temperature and heart rate during heat stress, in both the morning and afternoon, in recreationally active men. The study does not show the same effect in trained athletes or compare it with exercise heat acclimation.
paper.methods: Controlled laboratory study with 10 recreationally active men, who completed a 40-minute treadmill run at 65% VO2max in a 33 C chamber before and after six consecutive days of post-exercise hot water immersion (40 C, up to 40 minutes, performed 06:30 to 11:00). Exercise-heat tests were run at 09:45 and 14:45 on the same day. Paired t-tests and two-way repeated measures ANOVA were used, with a sample size estimate of eight participants plus dropout allowance.
paper.findings: Heat acclimation reduced resting rectal temperature (P = 0.002), rectal temperature at sweating onset (P = 0.001) and end-exercise rectal temperature (AM -0.47 C, PM -0.43 C; P = 0.001), as well as end-exercise heart rate (P < 0.001), RPE (P = 0.01), thermal sensation (P = 0.005), skin temperature and VO2. There were no heat acclimation by time-of-day interactions, so the changes were similar in morning and afternoon tests. Whole-body sweat rate, RER and plasma volume did not change.
paper.limitations: Small sample of 10 recreationally active men, with no women and no trained athletes. There was no concurrent control group; the comparison control data (thermoneutral immersion) come from an earlier study. The text lists mean RER both as having and as not having a time-of-day main effect, and the authors state that clock-time dependence of exercise heat acclimation still needs testing.
paper.practicalImplications: Post-exercise hot water immersion after morning exercise may be considered as a heat acclimation option when the time of day of future heat exposure is unknown, as in some military or occupational settings. The authors suggest it could be fitted into post-exercise washing routines, but the study did not test this in athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test sport performance or endurance outcomes. The authors call for trials in highly trained athletes that measure performance and heat illness.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study used healthy recreational men and does not address return to sport or heat-related injury.

records.sourceFile: Higher vs. Lower Intensity Strength Training Taper- Effects on Neuromuscular Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Pritchard HJ, Barnes MJ, Stewart RJ, Keogh JW, McGuigan MR. Higher vs. Lower Intensity Strength Training Taper: Effects on Neuromuscular Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018.
paper.abstract: Eleven strength-trained men completed a randomized crossover study with two four-week strength blocks, each followed by a one-week taper with about 70% lower volume and either higher or lower intensity. Countermovement jump height improved after training and again after the taper, isometric mid-thigh pull force improved after training, and there were no significant differences between the two tapers.
paper.tldr: In 11 strength-trained men, jump height kept improving during a one-week taper that cut volume by about 70%, while isometric strength was maintained rather than increased. Higher- and lower-intensity tapers did not differ significantly, so the study does not show that a higher-intensity taper is better.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover study in which 11 strength-trained men completed two four-week standardized strength blocks, each followed by a one-week taper that reduced volume by about 70%, with intensity increased by 5.9% (Taper A) or decreased by 8.5% (Taper B). Countermovement jump, isometric mid-thigh pull and isometric bench press were tested before training, after training and after the taper, with salivary hormones, creatine kinase and the DALDA questionnaire also measured; analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with effect sizes.
paper.findings: Pooled countermovement jump height rose from 38.0 cm (pre-training) to 39.3 cm (post-training, p = 0.010) and 40.0 cm (post-taper, p = 0.001), with a further post-training to post-taper gain (p = 0.002, pooled ES 0.14). Isometric mid-thigh pull relative peak force rose from 34.7 to 35.9 N/kg after training (p = 0.013) with no significant change across the taper. There were no significant between-taper or time-by-taper effects; within each taper, pre-training to post-taper effect sizes were small for jump height (0.43 higher-intensity, 0.30 lower-intensity) and mid-thigh pull (0.37, higher-intensity only).
paper.limitations: The study had only 11 participants and no untapered control group, so post-taper values reflect training and tapering together. The higher-intensity advantage was a non-significant trend based on within-taper effect sizes, the taper intensity changes (+5.9% and -8.5%) differed from the targets (+5% and -10%), accessory lifts were removed during tapers, and participants could continue their own aerobic or conditioning training. The manuscript is an accepted version without printed volume or page numbers, and dynamic strength was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In a one-week strength taper, a volume cut of about 70% with removal of accessory lifts preserved isometric strength and allowed a small further gain in jump height. The authors suggest trialing a slight intensity increase, but no between-taper difference reached statistical significance, so intensity choice is not settled by this study.
paper.athleteDev: In 11 strength-trained men, jump height improved slightly across a one-week taper that cut volume by about 70%, while isometric mid-thigh pull force, which rose during training, was maintained. A slightly higher-intensity taper showed a non-significant trend toward larger gains, and there was no untapered control.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested strength-trained men in a planned strength taper, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-training outcomes.
